title_angle: What Samarra preserves of the Abbasid world
thumbnail_visual_story: A surviving spiral minaret rises above unoccupied brick ruins on the right in warm daylight
facts: Samarra served as an Abbasid capital from 836 to 892.
It was the second Abbasid capital after Baghdad.
Its surviving plan helps researchers study an early Islamic capital.
The archaeological city preserves mosque and palace remains.
The Al-Malwiya and Abu Dulaf mosques form part of the site.
Carved stucco associated with Samarra influenced decoration elsewhere.
Early abandonment helped preserve the ancient city plan.
The remains are evidence of Abbasid architecture rather than a complete surviving city.

title_angle: Reading the layers of Islamic Cairo
thumbnail_visual_story: An unoccupied historic stone gateway frames a quiet courtyard on the right in clear daylight
facts: Cairo was founded as a Fatimid capital in 969.
Its historic fabric includes mosques, madrasas, baths and fountains.
The city expanded during the Mamluk period from 1250 to 1517.
Older settlements including Fustat became part of the wider urban fabric.
The Fatimid city forms a core of Historic Cairo.
The surviving gates include Bab Zuwayla, Bab al-Nasr and Bab al-Futuh.
The Ibn Tulun mosque dates from 876 to 879.
Historic Cairo was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1979.

title_angle: Why Baghdad mattered to Abbasid culture
thumbnail_visual_story: An empty brick archway opens onto an illustrative riverside cityscape on the right in soft daylight

source_records.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Art of the Abbasid Period

facts: The Abbasid dynasty succeeded the Umayyads in 750.
Abbasid political and cultural activity shifted eastward from Syria to Iraq.
Baghdad was founded in 762 as a new capital.
The circular city was known as the City of Peace.
Samarra later became an important Abbasid capital.
Little survives of the early Abbasid architecture of Baghdad.
Samarra therefore provides important surviving architectural evidence.
Abbasid art and architecture are studied through surviving objects as well as buildings.

title_angle: Good speech and care for neighbors
thumbnail_visual_story: A clay water jug and simple guest cups rest beside an empty doorway on the right in warm daylight
facts: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018 connects faith with conduct toward neighbors and guests and with speech.
The report is narrated by Abu Huraira.
It teaches avoidance of harm to a neighbor.
It teaches generous hospitality toward a guest.
It teaches good speech or silence.
The report appears in the collection section on good manners.
Modern applications should be identified as illustrations rather than additional prophetic statements.

The report is narrated by Anas.
It appears in the collection section on belief.

A contemporary example can illustrate reciprocity without being attributed to the Prophet.
